evidence.note: Opening frames the claim (shared array could undercut daytime power costs) and previews the 12-month pilot.
Problem: about 40% of electricity spend falls in daylight hours, with a £612 median yearly spend per flat; the saving that 40% implies per flat or per block is never stated.
Kicker says Problem but the slide reports 26 of 33 respondents support a pilot, before any pilot has been described; the resident quote is the only felt stake.
Resolution: 12-month pilot on blocks C and D, 64 kW, £86,400, Install -> 12 months measured -> Go or stop review.
Mechanism: shared array -> landlord supply -> flats' monthly credit; heavy daytime users get the largest credit, but no expected saving figure.
Risks and disputed payback (7 vs 11 years) are the only place the return on £86,400 appears.
Clear ask: board approves the £86,400 pilot with a go or stop review at twelve months.

rationale: The deck runs problem (s-2) through resolution (s-4, s-5), risks (s-6) and a clear ask (s-7), so the arc is present and ends well. But the stakes are only half concrete (the saving per flat or for the co-op is never quantified; payback appears only as a disputed risk), and s-3 jumps to survey support for a pilot before the pilot exists, under a Problem label. These order and transition weaknesses together fit level 3 better than level 4's single weak transition.
